title: God rested (Genesis 2:1–3)
hook: on the seventh day God stopped and blessed the stopping

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pentecost and ordinary time, and your line: the ordinary is holy. Did a chore turn into something more? That closed the circle of the year. Now ten days on sabbath and scripture. Day one hundred twenty-one.

When did you last stop? Not switch tasks. Not scroll on the couch while half-answering messages. Actually stop, with nothing left running. For a lot of people, the honest answer is: I can't remember. There's always one more email, one more load of laundry, one more thing. Now open the very first page of the Bible. Six days of making: light, sky, sea, land, stars, fish, birds, animals, people. Every day, something new. And then the seventh day comes, and the story says God does something that sounds almost strange for God. Nothing. On purpose. Today, the first stop in the Bible.
screen: `WHEN DID YOU LAST STOP?` → `SIX DAYS OF MAKING.` → `THEN, ON PURPOSE, NOTHING.`

segments.voice: Here's the text, in the King James Bible: "And on the seventh day God ended his work which he had made; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had made. And God blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it." The Hebrew word for rested is shavat. It means to stop, to cease. And from it comes the word sabbath, shabbat: the stopping. Notice: God doesn't rest because he's tired. Isaiah says God "fainteth not, neither is weary." The rest isn't recovery. It's a choice. The work is good, and finished, and so it's time to stop and enjoy it. Then something even stranger. God blesses the stopping. He makes the seventh day holy. The Jewish thinker Abraham Joshua Heschel pointed out that the first thing in the Bible God calls holy isn't a mountain or a temple. It's a day. A piece of time. Later, the commandment comes: "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy." And in Deuteronomy, it gets a second reason: you were once slaves in Egypt. Slaves can't stop. So rest is freedom, and it's for everyone in the house: children, workers, strangers, even the animals. Jews have kept that day for thousands of years, from Friday sundown to Saturday sundown, with candles, a meal and rest. Christians share this first page with them, and tomorrow we'll see how Christians came to keep their own day. But it all starts here: before any command to rest, God rests first, and calls it blessed.
screen: `SHAVAT: TO STOP.` · `NOT TIRED. FINISHED.` · `THE FIRST HOLY THING IS A DAY.` · `REST IS FREEDOM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stop completely. Put your phone face down, or out of reach, once the bell starts. Settle, and breathe. Don't plan. Don't fix. Don't review your list. If a task comes to mind, tell it: later. Just be here, doing nothing, on purpose. It may feel uncomfortable at first, even guilty. Let it. If you pray, you can rest in God, the way the seventh day did. If you don't, simply rest. Later today, stop again, for five whole minutes. The bell holds the time.
God rested. On the seventh day God stopped, and blessed the stopping, and made the day holy. Today's word.
Your line: rest is blessed. Today, stop completely for five minutes: no phone, no task, nothing. Day one hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: Christians read the seventh day of creation as the root of the sabbath and of their own day of rest; many set aside a weekly day for worship and rest, and Jews keep Shabbat from Friday sundown to Saturday sundown.
